standard.title: Creating Historical Arguments
standard.description: create descriptions, explanations and historical arguments, using historical knowledge, concepts and terms that incorporate and acknowledge evidence from sources
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can create descriptions, explanations and historical arguments using historical knowledge, concepts and terms that incorporate and acknowledge evidence from sources at Year 9 level.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create extended historical arguments that synthesise ideas, evaluate evidence, present a clear point of view, and are communicated for a specific purpose and audience in an appropriate form.

nodes.label: Constructing a historical argument
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct a historical argument that synthesises ideas, presents a particular point of view, and incorporates and evaluates available evidence.
nodes.minimum_width: Construct a historical argument that presents a clear position, incorporates evidence from at least two sources, and evaluates the strength of that evidence.
nodes.typical_width: Construct a historical argument that identifies different possibilities in interpretation, synthesises ideas to build an argument, presents a particular point of view that incorporates and evaluates available evidence; develop a historical explanation or interpretation using historical concepts and terms to build understanding of context, significance, purpose and the impact of the event or development.
wider: Construct a historical argument for a genuinely contested topic where the evidence is ambiguous or incomplete — practising how to acknowledge uncertainty while still presenting a clear, evidenced position

Develop a historical argument that incorporates First Nations perspectives and oral history sources alongside documentary evidence, evaluating how the inclusion of different source types affects the argument's evidential base and construction
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who can describe or explain but cannot synthesise and evaluate to construct an argument have not met the descriptor's demand — 'create... historical arguments... that incorporate and acknowledge evidence'. The difference between explanation and argument is the evaluative move — and without it, the extended text task of Node 2 cannot be completed at the required level.

response_modes.reason: Model the difference between historical explanation and historical argument explicitly: explanation answers 'what happened and why'; argument answers 'to what extent' or 'how significant' by evaluating competing possibilities and committing to a position supported by evidence.

success_criteria: Construct a historical argument that presents a clear, arguable position (not just a description or explanation)
Incorporate evidence from at least two sources and evaluate the strength of that evidence in relation to the argument
Use historical concepts and terms correctly throughout the argument

nodes.label: Extended historical text for purpose and audience
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop an extended historical text that explains, analyses and evaluates a historical event, development or movement for a specific purpose and audience, and can present historical arguments in a range of forms.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop an extended text that explains, analyses and evaluates a historical topic for a specific purpose and audience; present a historical argument in at least one chosen form.
nodes.typical_width: Develop an extended text that explains, analyses and evaluates a historical event, development or movement for purpose and audience — organising ideas and information to present relevant historical knowledge about the impact of a global event on a community to be presented to peers; present a historical argument in a chosen form: essay, oral presentation, debate, interactive digital or non-digital display, online conference or forum incorporating evidence.
wider: Produce a historical argument in an unfamiliar form — such as a museum exhibit text panel, a public lecture script, or a documentary voiceover — adapting historical communication to a specific purpose and audience different from a standard essay

Present a historical argument on a topic central to the course (e.g. the significance of Reconciliation, or the effects of post-war migration on Australian identity) using a form that requires the argument to be communicated to a non-specialist audience

response_modes.reason: This node integrates all S-strand skills — question development (S01), source work (S02–S04), causal and continuity analysis (S05), perspective analysis (S06), interpretation analysis (S07), and argument construction (Node 1) — into a complete, purposeful historical text. It is the culminating performance of the Year 10 historical skills sequence.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Presenting a historical argument in an unfamiliar form for a non-specialist audience is a high-demand transfer task that requires students to integrate all their historical skills while adapting their communication to a new context — a genuinely rich opportunity for advanced students.
success_criteria: Develop an extended historical text that explains, analyses and evaluates a historical topic — not merely describing it
Demonstrate a clear purpose and audience orientation in the organisation and communication of the text
Present the historical argument in a chosen form with appropriate structure, evidence, and use of historical concepts and terms
